name: anyMissing
title: Checks if there are any missing values in an object or not

origin.description: Checks if there are any missing values in an object or not. Please use base::anyNA() instead of anyMissing(), colAnyNAs() instead of colAnyMissings(), and rowAnyNAs() instead of rowAnyMissings().

arguments.name: x
arguments.text: A vector, a list, a matrix, a data.frame, or NULL.

arguments.name: idxs
arguments.text: A vector indicating subset of elements to operate over. If NULL, no subsetting is done.

origin.details: The implementation of this method is optimized for both speed and memory. The method will return TRUE as soon as a missing value is detected.
origin.value: Returns TRUE if a missing value was detected, otherwise FALSE.
origin.example:
x <- rnorm(n = 1000)
x[seq(300, length(x), by = 100)] <- NA
stopifnot(anyMissing(x) == any(is.na(x)))

translation.description: Checks if there are any missing values in an object or not. base anyNA covers the same question for a single array.

arguments.name: x
arguments.text: A NumPy array, a list, a dict of columns, or None. A double missing value is NaN. An integer missing value is None or the R integer NA sentinel.

arguments.name: idxs
arguments.text: A 1-based vector of elements to operate over. None selects every element.

translation.details: The scan is optimized for both speed and memory. It returns True as soon as a missing value is detected. Index rules from matrixStats validateIndices live in the anymissing crate. A list or dict is True when any element has a missing value.
translation.value: Returns True if a missing value was detected, otherwise False.
translation.example:
import numpy as np
from matrixstats.anymissing import anyMissing

x = np.random.default_rng(1).normal(size=1000)
x[299::100] = np.nan
anyMissing(x) == np.any(np.isnan(x))
